title: The continental drift theory
competency: Explain the continental drift theory, its evidence and why it was not easily accepted.

keywords.def: The theory that the continents have moved over geologic time across the earth's surface.
The single supercontinent from which the present continents were formed.
The northern part of Pangaea: North America, Europe and Asia (except India).
The southern part of Pangaea: South America, Africa, India, Australia and Antarctica.

en.text: The continental drift theory says the present continents were once one supercontinent, Pangaea. In the Triassic period of the Mesozoic era Pangaea split into Laurasia in the north and Gondwanaland in the south, which broke into today's continents and drifted to their present places over millions of years.

ideas.name: Evidence for drift and why Wegener was rejected

en.text: Alfred Wegener, a German meteorologist, proposed continental drift in 1912. His evidence: coastlines that fit, the same rocks and mountain belts across oceans, the same fossils (Mesosaurus) in South America and Africa, and matching ancient climates. Scientists rejected it mainly because he had no direct evidence of movement and no mechanism; plate tectonics later supplied one.

screens.title: A small reptile
screens.ask: Fossils of Mesosaurus, a small reptile, are found only in South America and in southern Africa. What does this suggest?
opts: The two continents were once joined
Two different reptiles evolved the same
screens.after: A small freshwater reptile could not cross an ocean, so the lands must once have been connected.

screens.title: Wegener's four evidences
paras: 1. Coastline fit: Africa and South America fit like a jigsaw, best at the continental shelves.
2. Rocks: the same rock types, of the same age, and the same mountain belts continue across.
3. Fossils: Mesosaurus found on both sides of the South Atlantic.
4. Palaeoclimate: rocks record the same ancient climates on now-distant continents.

screens.title: Why the theory was rejected
paras: Wegener was a meteorologist, not a geologist.
Leading scientists were in the north; his best data came from the south.
He thought the break-up began only in the Cenozoic: too little time.
Greatest problem: no direct evidence and no mechanism for moving continents.
His legacy: the shift from fixism to mobilism.
